questions.q: "Ecology" as a concept refers to:
o: The study of interactions between organisms and their environment
Only the study of climate change
questions.src: Ecology is the scientific study of interactions between living organisms and their surrounding environment.

questions.q: The "Biosphere" refers to:
o: A single ecosystem, like a forest
The global sum of all ecosystems — the zone of life on Earth
A legal term with no scientific meaning
questions.src: The biosphere is the sum total of all ecosystems on Earth, representing the entire zone supporting life.

questions.q: Which common law remedy is most commonly invoked for pollution causing smoke, noise, or odour affecting a neighbouring property's enjoyment?
o: Only criminal prosecution, never civil remedy
questions.src: Nuisance (public or private) is the classic common law tort remedy for interference with the use/enjoyment of land caused by pollution.

questions.q: The doctrine of Absolute Liability, applicable to hazardous industries under Indian law (as opposed to English Strict Liability), is characterised by:
o: Having the same exceptions as Rylands v. Fletcher
questions.src: Absolute Liability (established in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, 1987) admits no defences at all, unlike Strict Liability under Rylands v. Fletcher.

questions.q: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in:
questions.src: The Water Act 1974 was India's first major dedicated pollution-control statute, establishing Pollution Control Boards.

questions.q: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted primarily as a direct response to:
questions.src: The 1986 Act is the umbrella environmental legislation enacted in direct response to the devastating 1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy.

questions.q: The National Green Tribunal was established under the National Green Tribunal Act in:
questions.src: The NGT Act 2010 established this specialised tribunal for environmental case adjudication.

questions.q: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 was enacted to implement India's obligations under:
questions.src: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 implements India's obligations under the Convention on Biological Diversity (Rio, 1992).

questions.q: Article 48-A of the Indian Constitution is a:
o: Directive Principle of State Policy directing the State to protect and improve the environment
questions.src: Article 48-A is a Directive Principle (Part IV), non-justiciable but guiding State policy on environmental protection.

questions.q: Article 51-A(g) of the Constitution imposes a duty on citizens to:
o: Protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and have compassion for living creatures
questions.src: Article 51-A(g) is a Fundamental Duty specifically directed at environmental protection and compassion for living creatures.

questions.q: Courts in India have consistently held that the right to a clean and healthy environment falls within the scope of:
o: Article 32 exclusively, with no substantive right attached
Only Article 48-A, with no Fundamental Right dimension
questions.src: Judicial interpretation has firmly established the right to a clean environment as part of the Right to Life under Article 21.

questions.q: Both Article 48-A and Article 51-A(g) were inserted into the Constitution by which amendment?
questions.src: The 42nd Amendment 1976 inserted both Article 48-A (DPSP) and Article 51-A (Fundamental Duties, including 51-A(g)).

questions.q: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Ganga Pollution Case, 1988), the Supreme Court primarily established:
o: The Precautionary Principle for the first time
The Polluter Pays Principle and the right to a clean environment as part of Article 21
The Public Trust Doctrine for the first time
The doctrine of Absolute Liability for the first time
questions.src: This case established the Polluter Pays Principle and firmly linked environmental protection to Article 21, though the Precautionary Principle and Public Trust Doctrine came in later cases.

questions.q: In Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court formally adopted which TWO principles into Indian environmental law?
o: The Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle
Volenti non fit injuria and Necessity
questions.src: Vellore Citizens is the landmark case establishing both the Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle together in Indian jurisprudence.

questions.q: The Precautionary Principle, as recognised in Indian environmental law, holds that:
o: Preventive action should wait until complete scientific certainty of harm is established
Lack of full scientific certainty is NOT a valid reason to postpone preventive measures against serious/irreversible environmental harm
It applies only to water pollution cases
It has no bearing on the burden of proof in environmental litigation
questions.src: The Precautionary Principle allows preventive action even without complete scientific certainty, and shifts the burden of proving environmental safety to the developer/industry.

questions.q: The "Polluter Pays Principle" means that:
o: The government must always bear the cost of environmental cleanup
The party responsible for causing pollution must bear the cost of remediation and compensation, not the public
Only foreign companies are liable for pollution
Pollution costs are shared equally regardless of who caused them
questions.src: The Polluter Pays Principle places the financial responsibility for pollution remediation squarely on the party that caused it.

questions.q: The "Public Trust Doctrine," recognised in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, holds that:
o: Natural resources like rivers and forests are held by the State in trust for public benefit and cannot be alienated for purely private gain
The State owns all natural resources absolutely with no restrictions
Only private individuals can own natural resources
The doctrine applies only to mineral resources
questions.src: The Public Trust Doctrine restricts the State from transferring/alienating certain natural resources in a manner that defeats the broader public interest.

questions.q: "Sustainable Development" as a legal doctrine requires that:
o: Development must always be stopped in favour of environmental protection
Development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Environmental protection is irrelevant to economic policy
Only developed countries need to consider sustainability
questions.src: Sustainable Development balances economic growth with environmental preservation and inter-generational equity.

questions.q: The Taj Trapezium case primarily concerned:
o: Air pollution from nearby industries damaging the Taj Mahal's marble, resulting in orders to switch to cleaner fuel or relocate
questions.src: The Taj Trapezium case addressed industrial air pollution threatening the Taj Mahal, linking environmental law with cultural heritage protection.

questions.q: The Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, a foundational international environmental instrument, was adopted in:
questions.src: The Stockholm Declaration 1972 is widely regarded as the starting point of modern international environmental law, catalysing subsequent national legislative waves including in India.

questions.q: The Convention on Biological Diversity, associated with the "Earth Summit," was adopted at Rio de Janeiro in:
questions.src: The Rio Earth Summit 1992 produced the Convention on Biological Diversity, which India's own 2002 Biological Diversity Act implements domestically.

questions.q: The Kyoto Protocol, which set binding greenhouse gas emission reduction targets for developed countries, was adopted under the framework of:
o: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
questions.src: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) operates under the UNFCCC framework established in 1992.

questions.q: The Paris Agreement was adopted at which UN Climate Change Conference?
questions.src: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in 2015, committing signatories to limit global temperature rise through Nationally Determined Contributions.

questions.q: The Ramsar Convention (1971) primarily deals with the protection of:
o: Wetlands of international importance, especially as waterfowl habitat
questions.src: The Ramsar Convention 1971 is specifically focused on wetland conservation and their ecological importance, particularly for waterfowl.

questions.q: "Transboundary Pollution" under customary international law generally recognises that states have an obligation to:
o: Ignore environmental effects on neighbouring states
Prevent activities within their territory from causing significant environmental harm to other states or areas beyond national jurisdiction
Only cooperate with states sharing a land border
Compensate only for accidental pollution, never deliberate pollution
questions.src: Customary international environmental law recognises a state responsibility principle against causing significant transboundary environmental harm.
